newsitem.title: CANADA: Election dims hopes for Canada dollar rally.
newsitem.headline: Election dims hopes for Canada dollar rally.

text.p: The election of a regionally fractured Canadian parliament has dashed hopes that Canada's dollar might become a safe-haven currency for investors nervous about the prospects of European monetary union.

Economists had speculated that a big Liberal Party majority in Monday's election would spark a Canada dollar rally amid the chaos swirling around the European Union's proposed single currency, the euro.
But the governing Liberals were re-elected with a slender majority of just four seats in the new 301-seat parliament.
"This election is a long-term negative for the Canadian dollar," said Andrew Pyle, economist with ABN-AMRO Hoare Govett.
"We've got a major rift here with regional parties all over the place at a time when we're heading into a two-year horizon which will be much more focused on national unity and Quebec," he said.
Four other parties, including the separatist Bloc Quebecois and the Western Canada-based Reform Party, which advocates a tough line on concessions to Quebec, also won big blocks of seats.

Economists said the polarised parliament could trigger another constitutional crisis in Canada and play into the hands of Quebec's separatist government, which is expected to hold an election in 1998, followed by a sovereignty referendum in 1999.
Separatists narrowly lost a 1995 Quebec independence referendum by 50.6 percent to 49.4 percent.

Nagging doubts about the Canadian dollar, now worth about 72.74 U.S. cents, came on the heels of a run-up in its value against major European currencies. The dollar has been flat since the election results.
So far this year, the Canadian dollar has gained 12 percent against the German mark and French franc, due mostly to increased political instability in Europe.

An upset Socialist election victory in France and a controversial attempt by German Chancellor Helmut Kohl to revalue gold assets in Bundesbank reserves have put investors on the hunt for safe-haven currencies.
A decision on Tuesday by Sweden not to join the common currency by the 1999 deadline heightened uncertainty about the euro.
The U.S. dollar and the Swiss franc have been the most obvious beneficiaries of investor jitters, but traders have noted increased volumes of Canada dollar trading.
But those increased flows will dry up if Canada comes under a constitutional cloud, said Michael Gregory, economist and strategist with Lehman Brothers in Toronto.

"Canada may by default share in some of the U.S. dollar strength and gain against European currencies, but in the wake of the markets' slightly negative reaction to the election, Canada will not benefit disproportionately from turmoil in Europe," Gregory said on Wednesday.
He noted that the wild card for the Canadian dollar rested with Bank of Canada Governor Gordon Thiessen, who said last month that the central bank was adopting a less-stimulative monetary policy.
"If this turmoil in Europe persists into the period when the Bank of Canada begins to raise interest rates, then the Canadian dollar might get a bit of a boost," Gregory said.
